Anthropic Files for Potentially Largest IPO Ever Amid AI Safety Warnings

28 Oct 2026, 06:28 AM IST · GlobeWire Daily World Desk · Source: www.cbc.ca

Image: www.cbc.ca · Photo source · Cropped to 16:9; original source image

Overview

Anthropic, the San Francisco‑based artificial‑intelligence startup founded by former OpenAI leaders, filed a 335‑page registration statement on Monday that could set the stage for the biggest initial public offering (IPO) in history. The filing, made with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, outlines a plan to list on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker ANT and to raise as much as US$100 billion – a figure that would eclipse SpaceX’s record‑setting US$86 billion IPO earlier this year.

The filing arrives at a moment when the company’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, is publicly urging a slowdown in the development of ever‑more powerful AI models, warning that unchecked progress could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.” The juxtaposition of a massive capital raise with a stark safety warning has drawn attention from investors, regulators, and AI ethicists alike.

---

IPO Mechanics and Timeline

The registration statement sets the groundwork for an offering that could debut as early as next month. While the exact number of shares to be sold, the final offering price, and the ultimate valuation remain to be determined, analysts note that even a conservative estimate would place Anthropic among the world’s most valuable public companies.

Key points from the filing include:

  • Ticker: ANT on the Nasdaq Global Select Market.
  • Potential proceeds: Up to US$100 billion, according to media reports citing the filing.
  • Use of proceeds: The prospectus lists possible acquisitions, technology purchases, and infrastructure investments aimed at scaling the business and competing with rivals such as OpenAI, Google, and emerging Chinese AI firms.

Investors will receive a prospectus that, like most tech IPOs, contains a standard set of risk disclosures. As Earnest Wong, portfolio manager at Baskin Wealth Management, observed, “Most of the risks are kind of just normal, vanilla legal disclosures that are included in most companies.”

---

Financial Snapshot: Rapid Growth, Deep Losses

Anthropic’s filing reveals a company that is expanding quickly but has yet to achieve profitability. The firm reported a net loss of US$80.7 billion for the first half of 2026, a steep increase from a loss of US$13 billion in the same period a year earlier. Revenue is described as “growing rapidly,” though exact figures were not disclosed in the summary.

The loss figures underscore a broader trend in the AI sector, where the cost of compute, talent, and data is enormous. Anthropic, like OpenAI and SpaceX’s AI division, is spending heavily to develop large‑scale models, a strategy that has raised concerns about a potential AI‑related investment bubble.

---

Valuation Debate: From Private Funding to Public Markets

Private investors valued Anthropic at US$965 billion earlier this year. The IPO filing suggests that the market could assign a valuation between US$1.5 trillion and US$2 trillion, though the final number will depend on investor demand and the pricing of the offering.

Sinan Aral, professor at MIT’s Sloan School of Management, told CBC News, “It would instantly become one of the most valuable companies on the planet.” Yet Mark Daley, chief AI officer at Western University, cautioned, “Right now, investors are valuing hundreds of billions of dollars. And that may be right, but it’s also possible that a technology would transform our economy and also still be overvalued.”

The valuation question is not merely academic; it will affect the wealth of Anthropic’s founders, who collectively own roughly 500 million shares. Forbes estimates that Dario Amodei and his sister Daniela Amodei, Anthropic’s president, each hold a net worth of US$15.5 billion, placing them among the world’s 200 richest individuals.

---

Competitive Landscape: A Race for AI Dominance

Anthropic entered the market in 2021, positioning itself as a safety‑first alternative to other large AI labs. Its flagship chatbot, Claude, competes directly with OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini products. The rivalry between Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is often described as “bitter,” reflecting the high stakes of securing market share in a sector where compute resources and talent are scarce.

Beyond OpenAI, Anthropic faces competition from:

  • Google DeepMind and Google AI, which leverage the tech giant’s massive data centers.
  • Chinese AI startups backed by state funding.
  • SpaceX’s AI division, which, while primarily a space company, is investing heavily in AI for autonomous systems.

The IPO could provide Anthropic with the capital needed to expand its compute infrastructure, acquire complementary technologies, and attract top talent—critical moves in a field where the cost of training a single large model can run into the hundreds of millions of dollars.

---

AI Safety Concerns Embedded in the Prospectus

Perhaps the most striking element of the filing is the explicit acknowledgment that Anthropic’s models could “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.” This language mirrors statements made by CEO Dario Amodei in a recent essay urging the industry to pause the development of the most advanced models until safety measures catch up.

In September, Amodei warned that without a slowdown, AI could “let loose a swarm of agents that could take over the entire internet within six to 12 months.” He later wrote on his personal website, “I believe that if slowing down bought us even an extra year or two before models reach critical levels of capability, and we used that time to advance alignment, we could greatly reduce the risk that something goes seriously wrong.”

Anthropic has tried to brand itself as the “good guys” of AI, emphasizing responsible development and internal safety research. The prospectus lists typical corporate risks—staff retention, regulatory hurdles, and compute availability—but the existential‑risk clause stands out as a rare admission of the broader societal stakes.

---

Legal Battles and Government Scrutiny

Anthropic’s relationship with the U.S. government has been contentious. In February, the Trump administration labeled the company a “supply chain risk,” accusing it of endangering national security. Anthropic responded with two lawsuits:

  • A suit against the Pentagon alleging an “unlawful campaign of retaliation” after the firm refused unrestricted military use of its technology.
  • A separate case challenging a Pentagon rule that sought to designate Anthropic as a supply‑chain risk.

A California judge ruled in Anthropic’s favor in the first case, while a Washington, D.C., judge sided with the government in the second. Both decisions are under appeal, highlighting the uncertain regulatory environment for AI firms that straddle commercial and defense markets.

---

Potential Impact on Investors and the Public

If the IPO proceeds as projected, the influx of capital could:

  • Accelerate Anthropic’s product rollout, potentially expanding Claude’s availability to more enterprise customers.
  • Increase competition for compute resources, possibly driving up cloud‑provider prices.
  • Create a new class of ultra‑wealthy founders, reshaping the wealth landscape in the tech sector.

For everyday investors, the offering presents a classic high‑risk, high‑reward scenario. The company’s massive losses and the speculative nature of AI valuations mean that share price volatility could be extreme, especially as the market digests the dual narrative of massive growth potential and existential‑risk warnings.

  • The valuation range of US$1.5‑2 trillion discussed by analysts.
  • The existential‑risk language in the risk factors section of the prospectus.

---

Conclusion

Anthropic’s IPO filing signals a watershed moment for the AI industry: a company that has positioned safety at the core of its mission is now seeking a capital infusion of unprecedented scale. The juxtaposition of a potential US$100 billion raise with explicit warnings about existential threats underscores the dual nature of modern AI—simultaneously a driver of economic transformation and a source of profound societal risk.

Investors, regulators, and the public will be watching closely as the offering moves from filing to pricing. The outcome will not only shape Anthropic’s future but also set a benchmark for how the market values AI firms that openly acknowledge the stakes of their technology.
